en: Having explained the stage of completion (*utpannakrama*), he says "Now," and so forth, in order to explain its direct means, the stage of generation (*utpattikrama*).

Regarding the phrase "the miraculous display of all wheels" (*sarvacakravikurvitam*): because of the statement in the *Dvikalpa*, "They call the wheel (*cakra*) the mandala (*maṇḍala*)," [it refers to that].
In the *Dvikalpa*: "It takes (*lāti*) the essence (*maṇḍa*)," thus the meeting of the deities is the mandala.

The *kūṭāgāra* (pavilion) is the mandala because it is the support of the mandala; the *cakra* (wheel) is the assembly of deities whose nature is emptiness. The *kūṭāgāra* is the wheel because it is the support of the wheel; thus it is called the "mandala-wheel. Furthermore, this is because the assembly of deities consists of compassion and wisdom, and the *kūṭāgāra* is their locus—this is the explanation of the meaning. The *cakra* is the assembly of deities, and its "play" (*krīḍana*) consists of various emanations and so forth.

Of what nature is it? It is "universal" (*viśva*), meaning it possesses all forms (*viśvarūpa*) because it manifests a variety of immeasurable forms. It is "supreme" (*uttama*) because it demonstrates easy means for sentient beings according to their respective capacities. Where, then, is this to be accomplished? He states the locus: "in the secret" (*rahasye*). "Secret" refers to the interior of the vajra-cage and, as appropriate, the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*). We shall explain where each of these is situated as appropriate.
Furthermore, other meanings have been explained, such as that beginning with "the supreme" (*paramādika*).
As for the question of where one should remain, he says: "in solitude," and so forth.

He explains the *vikurvitam* (miraculous manifestation) that was previously mentioned, beginning with the words "from all sides" (*sarvataḥ*). The term *sarvatoviśvamudrā* refers to the yogin who possesses the form of the deity, for he seals the entire universe in all its aspects, such as the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth. From all sides, through various forms of utterly pure bliss resulting from the enjoyment of sense objects, he should perform what is beneficial for all sentient beings in every direction, according to their individual capacities. This is because the welfare of beings is accomplished through bliss alone by means of meditation; thus, unlike one following the *pāramitā* vehicle, there is an absence of suffering such as the cutting off of hands and feet.

Why, then, is this which consists of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) not cultivated? It is indeed cultivated. For it is called a *maṇḍala* because it takes—that is, grasps—the *maṇḍa*, the essence; [it is] the very gnosis of emptiness (*śūnyatā-jñāna*), because it takes up the essence of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) in which emptiness and compassion are inseparable. And it is said in the *Samājottara*:
"The vulva is declared to be the *maṇḍala*, and the thought of awakening is the *maṇḍala*."
"The body is said to be the mandala; thus is the conceptualization of the three mandalas.
And in the *Abhidhānottaratantra*:
[Q/R *Abhidhānottara* (chapter 53)]
The maṇḍala is the supreme reality, the highest gnosis of Śrī Heruka.
The maṇḍala is the vulva-lotus, the supreme arising from the body of Vārāhī.
The maṇḍala is the union therein; the maṇḍala is the supreme bliss.
"The maṇḍala of the Vīra and Yoginī is the supreme non-dual union.
Thus it is said that among the maṇḍalas of the body, the bhaga, and the bodhicitta, it is the bodhicitta itself [that is the maṇḍala].
(From the *Guhyendumaṇitilaka*)
Transcending the cultivation of all limbs, free from conceptual construction and its objects, and beyond measure and the bindu— this is the supreme essence (*maṇḍa*).
Thus it is said in the *Sarvatathāgatakāyavākcittaguhyālaṃkāravyūha-mahātantra*:
"In the *Sarvatathāgatakāyavākcittaguhyālaṃkāravyūha-maṇḍala*, the knowledge of emptiness of all Mothers is taught."
"What shall I teach that is devoid of all conceptual constructions?
Thus it is said in the *Vajramaṇḍālaṃkāra-mahātantra*.
"When the mind has arisen as something inconceivable, without appearance, unclouded, and beyond syllables— empty and equal to space—
then the seals, mantras, and deities are conceptually constructed."
Intending this very point, Kahnapāda said: "Who is the Tathāgata? [It is] the goddess Koṃī together with the hosts of gods."
"Remain as mandala-circles through the moments of coemergence"—thus [it is said].

Regarding "among the deities," this refers to the other deities. By this, it is stated that the body-mandala, which consists of the forms of the deities whose nature is bodhicitta inseparable from emptiness and compassion, effects the welfare of the world through the emanations of various deities. Because it illuminates that [mandala], the powder mandala (*rajomaṇḍala*) is also called a "mandala."

Now, is it not taught—that even for those to be trained—it is taught that one’s own mind, which is naturally pure and the bearer of manifold dharmas, is itself the maṇḍala? For even when the yogin of purified mind radiates in the form of a maṇḍala, and even though it is presided over by perfectly pure Buddhas, it is because of the very awakening to natural purity [that this occurs]. Indeed, it is through the awakening to the natural purity of one’s own mind alone that one becomes a Buddha or a yogin, even in a partial sense.

Therefore, even if it is said that the maṇḍala consists entirely of pure dharmas, nevertheless, this does not contradict the fact that it takes the form of the minds of all sentient beings. [The opponent objects: "If this is so, there would be no purpose whatsoever in teaching the stage of generation (*utpattikrama*). [The author replies: "If there is another [purpose], let it be stated. To this he says: "What [is it]? The meaning is that there is nothing that cannot be accomplished through the method of the intrinsic nature of the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*). As for the stage of generation and so forth that I have described—

This drama was performed by the Buddha Vajrasattva for the very benefit of those of gentle disposition and beginners, in order to conform to their minds. Indeed, displaying his creative play (*prapañca*) through various emanations of form—rendered beautiful by diverse costumes, ornaments, and arrangements—he manifests as many while being one, and as one while being many; and demonstrating the nature of appearance and disappearance, he enacts a dance for the assembly of Buddhas such as Vairocana and others, for the sake of those disciples to be trained.

"He manifests" refers to his wondrous drama of diverse, inconceivable, and emanated forms. For beginners, through the accumulation of merit, their wisdom becomes superior; having gained confidence through the attainment of worldly fruits, they apply themselves with even greater diligence to the cultivation of the generation stage (*utpannakrama*). However, this should not be contemplated at the outset for those of dull intellect who are unable to comprehend such a purpose.

For having heard that everything is accomplished through the cultivation of the completion stage (*utpannakrama*) alone, those who are incapable in that regard fall away even from the generation stage (*utpattikrama*). Therefore, for their sake, the cultivation of the generation stage itself is taught as the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). The meaning is that there is no harm even in contemplating [the generation stage] through the knowledge of the aforementioned relationship between cause and effect. For this very reason, they declare that even one who has understood the completion stage should cultivate the generation stage first, while taking into account the necessity of [further] maturation.

Meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) consists of the seed-syllables, signs, and so forth; from these arises the yoga of the deity. The mantra to be recited begins with *oṃ*. The sequence of their ritual procedure will be explained below. By the phrase "the miraculous transformation of the mind," he indicates that all of this must be performed through the very resolve (*adhimokṣa*) that the nature of form is the essence of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*). For all of this is included within the five families, such as Vairocana and the others, and those [families] are one and the same Vajradhara, whose self-nature is the thought of awakening. "The Śūnyavajrin" refers to the Śūnyavajrī.

This has been stated: the Blessed Lord Vajrasattva himself, whose nature consists of wisdom (*prajñā*) and means (*upāya*), assuming a conventional form through the aspects of the five Tathāgatas, the Vidyās, and so forth—whose essence is passion (*rāga*) and the rest—acts for the sake of purifying the minds of the realm of sentient beings who are enveloped by afflictions. By enjoining those very disciples who are capable of entering such a path into reality (*tattva*), he remains thus even though he is free from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). As it is said in the *Ḍākinīvajrapañjara*:
"O you who are hatred, delusion, suchness, pride, passion, and envy toward people..."
To gather [beings], the Vajra-holder himself assumed manifold forms;
for by whatever disposition the minds of men are joined,
he becomes composed of that very thing, like a gem of universal color.
Therefore, with every effort, one should purify the vajra of the mind;
when the mind is pure, there arises bliss that destroys the poison of all afflictions.
This was also stated by the venerable Āryadeva:
In the *Svādhiṣṭhānakramasūtra*, that which is taught as the great family of the five Buddhas,
as well as the various deities born from each of those respective families—

The male and female messengers, as well as the wrathful deities, the female servants, the male servants, and the attendants—these do not exist, nor do they exist; they are manifested for the sake of sentient beings.
The yogi should emanate all of this and also withdraw it back into himself.

"Abiding in the illusion-like samādhi, [he manifests] mandalas as well in detail. *Mahāsurata* means one who possesses great passion (*mahāsukha*), or one who is exceedingly devoted to the great welfare of others. For this very reason, he is a "supreme lord" (*suprabhu*). Regarding "the form and color of the generation stage": by way of the generation stage, "color" (*varṇa*) refers to the syllable (*akṣara*), and "form" (*rūpa*) refers to blue and so forth. "First" (*prathama*) means being first in relation to compassion and the other [immeasurables]. This is for the purpose of making compassion and the rest manifest effortlessly through the power of loving-kindness (*maitrī*). As for that which is to be meditated upon first, he will state later: "one should first meditate on that which is the first, such as a corpse," and so on.
The characteristics of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the other [immeasurables] have already been explained.

Thus, immediately after the arising of the conventional mind of awakening (*sāṃvṛtabodhicitta*), he speaks of the ultimate [mind]. The phrase "once again" means according to the sequence beginning with the first [stage]. One should follow the instruction regarding the selflessness (*nairātmya*) of all phenomena through their being devoid of a nature of unity or multiplicity (*ekāneka-svabhāva-viyoga*) and so forth; one should first meditate on awakening (*bodhi*) of that nature—this is the connection. The intention is that the realization of great bliss (*mahāsukhābhisambodhi*) comes later.

Regarding "the gathering of the seed" (*bījasaṃgraha*): one should meditate upon the "gathering," that is, the correct grasping, of the seed which is the cause for the arising of the deity. In this context, the "seed"—following the awakening to emptiness and immediately after death—is the sprout of the bodhicitta inseparable from emptiness and compassion in the form of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). This is appropriately interspersed with syllables such as *hūṃ* or the pair of *hoḥ*s. Its "gathering" consists in its abiding within the enclosure of the vajra-fence and so forth, or between the moon and sun, or between the father and mother, or between the vajra and the lotus. "The image" (*bimba*) refers to the form of the deity.

"Placement is the syllable" means the placement of syllables (*akṣaranyāsa*). This refers to the placement of syllables within the four wheels and in the heart; it is also an elliptical expression for the placement of the sense faculties (*indriyanyāsa*) and the placement of the lords of the families (*kuleśanyāsa*).

Having thus indicated the ultimate *bodhicitta* with its four limbs, he describes the surrounding enclosure, beginning with "by the letter *ra*" and so forth. The universal vajra (*viśvavajra*), which is of a nature serving as a support, is as vast as desired; it constitutes the wall and the cage-binding. That is to say, the vajra-wall, the vajra-cage, and the boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*).

There, from the illumination of those vast rays, one should visualize a boundary-binding consisting of flames all around; and from the seed-syllable situated in its center, one should visualize a vajra-fence and a vajra-canopy formed by a dense, thick, and immovable mass of emanating vajras.

This preparation follows immediately after the realization of emptiness. He speaks of the preparation that is to be performed first, beginning with the words "First," and so forth. A corpse (*mṛtaka*) is a dead body. Because it is devoid of a self, and because it illuminates the *dharmadhātu*, it has the *dharmadhātu* as its essence. "Having remained" means having resolved (*adhimucya*) upon oneself as remaining [in that state]. "Consisting of wisdom and skillful means" is because its intrinsic nature is the bodhicitta of emptiness and compassion. This is the procedure common to all [practices] following the yoga, as appropriate.

Concerning the *Herukakrama*, it says: "From the syllable HŪṂ," and so forth. "Arising from the vajra" means the production of the vajra. The *varaṭa* is the central sphere. The syllable HŪṂ itself is the reality (*tattva*). Having the nature of hatred (*dveṣātmaka*) means having the essence of artificial wrath for the sake of destroying the faults of the wicked. "Vajra-janma" refers to Hevajra. "With faith" means with inclination. It is blue, or with a reddish-blue luster, in order to indicate great compassion and passion.

Thus, having instantly visualized oneself in the form of Heruka, and with one’s self purified, one should see the Lord in the sky, drawn there by rays from the seed-syllable in one’s own heart, and worship him with the eight goddesses who have emerged from the seed-syllable in one’s own heart. *Mṛgalāñchana* is the moon; *mārtaṇḍa* is the sun; *bhaiṣajya* is Vairocana; *vajra* is meat. However, in the reading *gandhahasta*, "scent" (*gandha*) here refers to meat, as he will say: "a skull-cup full of meat. *Rasa* is wine.

Therein, the *ḍamaru* [drum] is the outer worship; the secret worship is with the essences of the five nectars; but the worship of reality consists of great bliss (*mahāsukha*). Embracing the neck with great passion, the *ḍombī* performs [the rite].

He explains the awakening to emptiness that was previously indicated, beginning with the words "therefore" (*tataḥ*) and so forth. A "footstep" (*pada*) is a resolve or conceptual construction; being "devoid" (*vinirmukta*) of that means its absence, which is emptiness (*śūnyatva*). That which has all phenomena as its self is "consisting of all phenomena" (*sarvadharmātmaka*). However, the taking of refuge and so forth are not indicated here, because this [practice] is intended for those of superior faculties (*adhimātra*). For them, since everything is already well-established through the very entry into the mandala, they maintain it in exactly that way.

Nevertheless, for the sake of ensuring that even those [karmic traces] do not perish, and for the sake of favoring those of dull faculties, one should introduce [the practice] from another tantra. Immediately thereafter, the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) are to be cultivated; after that, emptiness; and after that, the vajra-fence. This sequence should also be understood according to the specific requirements in other yoga systems. Particular details—such as the seed-syllable and its emblem, the form of the chosen deity resulting from their transformation, and the worship of the chosen deity—are to be inferred [from other sources].

Immediately following that, he describes what is to be meditated upon within the interior of the vajra-fence, in the midst of the eight cremation grounds clearly perceived, situated upon the heart of a corpse at the center of a multicolored lotus petal, on a solar seat: "The row of moons," and so forth. The *āli* transformed into the form of the moon is the "row of moons" (*candrāli*). The sun transformed by the *kāli* is the "sun of the *kāli*" (*kālimārtaṇḍa*). The seed-syllable *hūṃ* is to be meditated upon in the center of the union of the sun and moon.

That very seed-syllable, which is the *sattva* abiding within the space between the moon and sun of the parents and whose nature is supreme bliss (*paramānanda*), is what they call [the deity]. The meaning is that it is this very thing that is cultivated here as the object of the "innate" (*sahaja*). Regarding "the appearance of one's own body": from the seed-syllable situated upon the vajra-umbilicus produced by the transformation of that seed, there arise the bodies of the deities, which resemble the Vajra-body, are blue in color, possess the flavor of wrath (*krodharasa*), and serve as the means for disciplining the world. "In the heart" refers to the seed-syllable. Furthermore, the application of the sequence of the fivefold awakening (*pañcākārābhisambodhi*) mentioned here should also be understood as it will be explained later.

Thus, through the transformation of the moon, sun, and vajra seeds, Hevajra, whose nature is hatred and who consists of supreme bliss, arises together with his retinue generated from their respective seed-syllables. Regarding the passage beginning with "in the element of space" (*khadhātāv*) and ending with "blue and reddish-glowing" (*nīlāruṇābham*), this section should be understood as immediately following the phrase "consisting of the essence of all phenomena" (*sarvadharmātmakam*). The remainder of the text is: "the vajra born from the syllable *hūṃ*."

He explains what kind of Hevajra one should meditate upon with the words beginning "all," and so forth. The ornaments are: the five skulls on the head, the wheel, the earrings, the necklace, the girdle, the ashes, and a garland of fresh human heads. The garment is a tiger skin, which, when accompanied by a consort (*saprajña*), is placed only behind [her]. Having placed the right foot upon the left thigh, he is in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅkin*). His eyes are red and round. Bhairava is a corpse of terrifying form.

He holds a vajra-khaṭvāṅga like a sacred thread (yajñopavīta). He holds a skull-cup filled with great blood and marked with a vajra. He brandishes a black five-pronged vajra adorned with a garland of flames. His nature is utterance; his habit is utterance.

"Śmaśāna" means "dwelling" (*vasana*) or "abode" (*nivāsa*), because they dwell therein; thus, it is a dwelling for corpses (*śava*). In this term, there is the substitution of *mat* for the initial part of the first member, and the elision of *va* for the initial part of the second member. This is according to etymological derivation (*nirukta*) through phonetic modification. Therein, their activity of dwelling consists of walking, standing, lying down, and sitting, respectively upon headless trunks, hanging corpses, those lying on their sides, and those pierced by stakes. This is the intended meaning.

Just as corpses in a charnel ground are devoid of self, so too is every place; thus, the "charnel ground" refers to all abodes of sentient beings being devoid of self. Sentient beings are empty of the intrinsic nature of a sentient being, and the abodes of sentient beings are also empty of the intrinsic nature of an abode of sentient beings—this is the meaning of "charnel ground. Therefore, it is fitting that the play of the Blessed One—who is of the nature of the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*) consisting of non-referential great compassion and great wisdom—occurs within that very *ālaya*.

The goddesses are Vajra-raudrī and the others; thus, he is surrounded by sixteen goddesses. In this way, the accomplishment of the four-armed and six-armed forms is also achieved. The specific details should be understood as stated in the Tantra.
Furthermore, the armor-mantras (*kavaca*) and so forth to be described later should be known.

Even in this case, when practicing the meditation on the two-armed form, the attainment of Mahāmudrā is indeed possible, because at the beginning and at the conclusion of the session, one recollects the application of the mudrās, just as in the meditation on Nairātmyā.

For instance, once the Blessed One together with his retinue has been accomplished, following the entry of the Knowledge-Beings (jñānasattva), the empowerment, the sealing, the worship, the praise, and the tasting of nectar, the exceedingly joyful Yoginīs—manifesting their inner disposition through side-long glances, praise, gestures, speech, and so forth—approach the Blessed One and, out of the intensity of their passion, perform the act of the man (puruṣāyita), having reached a state of horripilation, trembling, and other such physical responses.

Then, first of all, Pṛthvīvajrā embraces [the practitioner], and thereafter the others enter her; thus, in this context, she indeed kindles the innate great bliss (*sahajamahāsukha*). This sequence should be understood accordingly in other cases as well. This is the procedure in brief.

The central [deity], however, is as before during the meditation on the corpse and so forth within the interior of the peaked pavilion situated upon the universal vajra on the lotus inside the *dharmodayā*. The detailed [procedure], however, should be understood from the sequence beginning with the melting [of the moon] following the central meditation, once the maṇḍala lords and the retinue have been generated, just like the sixteen-armed [Heruka]. Some masters maintain that the Blessed One Trailokyākṣepa is to be inferred as being in union with Nairātmyā; but primarily, according to the section on the abbreviated rite, he is Heruka.

The maṇḍala of Selflessness (nairātmyāmaṇḍala) is by virtue of the medium procedure; the eight-faced maṇḍala is by virtue of the superior procedure. "All-nectar" (sarvasāmṛta) refers to the nectar-procedure that fulfills all the yogas to be described hereafter.

He speaks in order to state the specific characteristics of the four-armed [deity], beginning with "sa eva" (he himself), and so forth. He is of the nature of the four joys (*caturānanda*) because he arises as the single flavor (*ekarasa*) of the four joys. Through that very nature, there is the conquest and purification of the four Māras; and by means of that, he possesses four arms. Regarding the phrase "samāliṅgitavigraham" (with his body embraced): his body (*vigraha*) is embraced by Wisdom (*prajñā*); one should meditate upon him as such.

In order to state the specific details of the six-armed [Heruka], he says "first," and so forth. "Empty" (*śūnya*) is an elliptical expression for the remaining ritual procedure. Vajrasattva is partless (*niṣkala*), because from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), he cannot be conceptualized due to being devoid of all proliferation (*prapañca*). To the question "How so?", he says "in the moon," and so forth. In the meditation on the six-armed form, the syllable *hūṃ* has the nature of the Causal Vajradhara, and thus possesses a lunar disc. However, the three Herukas who are the Resultant forms possess solar discs.

[He holds] the skull-bowl filled with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), which is unsmeared, black, and wrathful. By virtue of the word "and" (*cakāra*), the fifth [nectar], *amṛta*, is included. He holds in his left hands the vajra-bell, the bow, and the skull-cup; in his right hands, the vajra, the arrow, and the trident. His consort is Vajraśṛṅkhalā, who has the form of the Blessed One (the Buddha). She embraces him with her two hands, which hold a vajra and a vajra-bell. Regarding the phrase "in the center of the *bhaga*": *bhaga* refers to the *dharmodayā*.

The meaning is that one should meditate upon the Blessed One together with his consort within the interior of a celestial palace (kūṭāgāra) situated upon a universal vajra, which rests on a lotus arising from the source of phenomena (dharmodayā) surrounded by cremation grounds, all within the interior of a vajra-fence; specifically, [he is seated] upon a sun disc atop a skull-cup filled with blood, which is located at the heart of a corpse standing upon the pericarp of a universal lotus. This is to be done in a manner that is "joined" (*yukta*), meaning properly integrated.

"One should visualize the deities" refers to the male deities such as Vaṃśa and the female deities; this indicates the general instruction. "By means of the two petals" means that one should draw eight goddesses upon the eight petals; the implication is that the same applies to the mandala to be drawn. On the eastern petal is Vajraraudrī, white in color: in her left hands she holds a bow and a skull-cup, and in her right hands an arrow and a goad. On the southern [petal] is Vajrabimbā, yellow: in her right hands she holds a trident and a vajra, and in her left hands a skull-cup and a noose.

In the west is Vajrarāgī, red in color; she holds a sword and a vajra in her two right hands, and a skull-cup and a bell in her two left hands. In the north is Vajrasaumyā, green in luster; others say she is *sumuṇḍī* (or *musuṇḍī*), a crusher, and green. [The mudrā is formed by] contracting the little fingers and thumbs, while the three middle fingers are raised as the *tripatākā*. In the northeast is Vajrayakṣī, white-yellow; in the southeast is Vajraḍākinī, yellow-red. Regarding the placement of the hand symbols for the three starting with Vajrasaumyā, they are placed in the left and right hands respectively.

In the southwest is Śabdavajrā, red-blue; in the northwest is Pṛthvīvajrā, green-white. The four [emblems]—the flask, the vajra, the bell, and the skull-cup—are the symbols in the two right and two left hands of these two goddesses respectively. The substance is the five nectars. He concludes with the words "from the two petals," and so forth. Mahāsukha is Vajradhara. "With musical instruments" means the goddess is accompanied by musical instruments. There, outside the eight-petaled goddesses, is Vaṃśā in the northeast and Vīṇā in the southeast.

In the southwest is Mukundā; in the northwest is Murajā. These four have two arms, three eyes, and one face. Playing their respective musical instruments with both hands, they wear crowns of matted hair (*jaṭāmakuṭinī*) and perform the *tāṇḍava* dance in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*). Their colors are, respectively, red, yellow, white, and smoky-grey. At the eastern gate is Vajrāṅkuśī, dark blue like the sky; her right face is black and her left is white. In her three right hands, she holds a hook (*aṅkuśa*), a sword (*khaḍga*), and a wheel (*cakra*).

In her left hands are a noose, a threatening gesture (*tarjanī*), and a bell. She is white and yellow; her right face is black and her left is red. In her right hands are a noose, a vajra, and a sword; in her left hands are a wheel, a bell, a threatening gesture, and a noose. To the west is Vajrasphoṭā, who is red; her right face is black and her left is white. In her right hands are a vajra-shackle and a vajra-sword; in her left hands are a wheel, a bell, and a goad (*aṅkuśa*).
In the north is Vajraghaṇṭā, who is green; her right face is black and her left is white. In her right hands she holds a bell, a vajra, and a sword; in her left hands, a wheel, a goad, and a noose.

These sixteen goddesses have red, circular, three-eyed faces and gaze toward the Lord. They are adorned with a wheel of five skulls upon their heads, anklets, and other ornaments; they wear tiger-skin garments and perform the *tāṇḍava* dance with the nine dramatic sentiments (*navanāṭyarasa*). Except for the four goddesses of the flute and so forth who stand above the sun held in blood-filled skull-cups, the others have flaming, tawny hair tied upward. Beneath the skull-cups of the eight [goddesses], including the flute-player and others, are double-lotuses (*viśvapadma*). Therein, the female gatekeepers stand in the *pratyālīḍha* posture.
The others [should sit] in the half-lotus posture. He concludes: "One should meditate on [it] in the center of the bhaga."

*Oṃ āḥ hūṃ hrīḥ svāhā* is the mantra for recitation (*jāpyamantra*) for each of the three forms of Heruka with two arms and so forth; however, the specific mantras for each will be stated later. The same applies to the sixteen goddesses. The single-syllable seed-mantra of origination (*utpattibīja*) is *hūṃ* for the Blessed One together with his consort (*saprajña*), and *hrīḥ* for the goddesses of the petals. For the eight [goddesses] beginning with Vaṃśā, they are, in order: *oṃ oṃ eṃ aiṃ jaḥ hūṃ baṃ hoḥ*. The phrase "endowed with the four seed-syllables" and so forth is the general indication (*uddeśa*) of the mantra for recitation, while *oṃ āḥ oṃ haṃ svāhā* and so forth is the detailed explanation (*nirdeśa*).

The "primordial vowel" (*ādisvara*) is the syllable *oṃ* of the fourfold mantra. That which has this as its beginning is "beginning with the primordial vowel," namely the syllable *āḥ*. The mantra distinguished by that is as will be specified: *oṃ āḥ vajrāṅkuśi jaḥ haṃ svāhā*, and so forth.

He states the mantra for the empowerment of the vajra and lotus, beginning with "Then," and so forth. One should "establish" means one should visualize. One should utter the vajra as *hūṃ jaṃ*, empowered by the syllable *hūṃ* and having its tip empowered by the syllable *oṃ*. The lotus is transformed from *hrīḥ* and is empowered by that [syllable], with its tip empowered by the syllable *āḥ*. In external passion (*bāhyarate*) as well, when a man and woman who are deeply attached perform the festival of sexual union, one should take with the mouth and consume the emitted semen—due to the power of meditative concentration (*dhāraṇā*)—in this very context.
As it is said in the *Vajrāmṛtatantra*: [The passage continues with the citation from the *Vajrāmṛtatantra*.]
One should not extract it from that place with the two hands or with the fingers;
if a fool acts thus, having extracted it, he perishes.
One should always take it with the mouth itself, and likewise with the graceful tongue.

He states that this worship is supreme: "One should worship with perfumes and flowers, with semen and blood. According to the interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*), this refers even to external perfumes and so forth. "The *bhaga*" is an indicative term for wisdom (*prajñā*). "Recitation" (*jāpa*) refers to the vajra-recitation and others to be described later. In that very context, through the union of the vajra and the lotus as previously stated—in the *Advayasamatāvijaya*:
"Having established the *liṅga* in the *bhaga*, one should recite the mantra again and again."
"The yogi should always emanate mandalas from mandalas.
This is the sequence of realization for these three mandalas, beginning with the two-armed one.

First, having visualized oneself as Heruka residing upon a corpse, arisen from the *repha*, the sun, and the *hūṃ* that produces the vajra, one should worship the Lord (Bhaṭṭāraka), who has been drawn forth by rays from the seed-syllable in the heart, together with the eight goddesses. Then, having performed the confession of sins and so forth, up until the stage of equanimity (*upekṣā*), one should meditate on emptiness, thinking: "I am of the nature of the Vajra of the Wisdom of Emptiness" (*oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*). Next, having contemplated the *repha*, the syllable *ja*, the *va*, the *hūṃ*, the crossed-vajra (*viśvavajra*), its rays, and so forth, [one should place them] upon the sun at the heart of a corpse on a universal lotus in the midst of the eight cremation grounds.

One should visualize [the deity] arisen from the transformation of the *āli* and *kāli*, the moon, the sun, the syllable *hūṃ*, the vajra, and another *hūṃ*, surrounded by a circle of goddesses born from their respective seed-syllables, with two, four, or six arms. Then, one should contemplate Mohavajrī, Dveṣavajrī, Mātsaryakī, Rāgavajrī, and Īrṣyāvajrī in the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind respectively; and Khecarī, Bhūcarī, and Nairātmyā in the body, speech, and mind. These [deities] are black, holding a curved knife and a skull-cup in their hands, and are situated upon the moon.

In the *nirmāṇacakra* and the other wheels, there are the syllables OṂ HŪṂ OṂ HAṂ, which are blue, black, red, and white respectively. Thereafter, having summoned the maṇḍala of the *jñānasattva* by means of rays from the seed-syllable in the heart, preceded by the offering water (*argha*) and foot-washing water (*pādya*) empowered by the mantra at one's own heart, one unifies it with the *samaya-maṇḍala* through the recitation of JAḤ HŪṂ BAṂ HOḤ—by means of summoning, entering, binding, and subjugating. Then, having drawn in the Buddhas with rays from the seed-syllable in the heart, one worships them with the eight Mothers.

Following the prayer, "Oṃ! May the Tathāgatas consecrate me," one is consecrated and sealed by those five nectar-vases (*pañcāmṛta-kalaśa*). In this regard, the Blessed Lord and the Blessed Lady are [sealed] by Akṣobhya; Vajraraudrī and the others, however, are [sealed] by Akṣobhya and the rest who will be described in the Vajrasattva-maṇḍala. This is the Ādiyoga. Thereafter, one should taste the nectar according to the ritual procedure.
(Hevajratantra II.ii.30)
Just as an illusion, just as a dream, and just as the intermediate state may be,
so too does the mandala appear through the yoga of constant practice.
Thus is the Samādhi of the Supreme King of Mandalas (maṇḍalarājāgrī).

Thereafter, one should visualize within one’s own body the world as having been made fully awakened through the emanations of the mandala-circles beginning with the Tathāgata, according to the appropriate method; and within the goddess embraced by oneself, one should visualize the other yoginīs.

And as he experiences the bliss of passion with her, the moon-drop (śaśībindu), burnt by the radiance of the fierce fire of Caṇḍālī—which has the form of straight lines impelled by the wind of exhalation from the navel—is heard together with the breath-wind and becomes one with Caṇḍālī. Experiencing innate bliss (*sahajasukha*), it gradually descends toward the navel-center and becomes supportless. Thus, again and again. Then, having focused on the wind restrained at the navel, one should perceive only the drop (*bindu*).

One should instantly visualize the mandala circle as fully manifested within the center of that drop. One should meditate upon that very mandala circle as being composed of illusion; this is the King of Rituals Samādhi (karmarājāgrī-samādhi).
Due to weariness from meditation, one should recite the respective mantras to be described below.

Alternatively, immediately after the meditation on the vajra-fence, one should visualize—instantly appearing within the *dharmodayā* transformed from one’s chosen deity—inside a *viśvājña* (universal lotus), upon the pericarp and a *viśvavajra* altar, the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*) produced from the wind-mandala and so forth according to the ritual procedure, surrounded by the eight cremation grounds which indicate the selflessness of all world-realms; the rest is as before.
The seventh mañjarī in the *Āmnāyamañjarī*, a commentary on the *Śrīsampuṭa*.
